extracted.intended_audience: attorneys and agents who practice before the USPTO (patent/trademark practitioners), OED counsel, and adjudicators in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used in USPTO disciplinary proceedings assessing practitioner misconduct (signatures, cooperation with OED, specimen authenticity, mens rea, and sanctions). Useful for evaluating alleged violations of the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct and determining sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to discipline and applicable procedural framework
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has exclusive authority to establish qualifications for admitting persons to practice before it and to suspend or exclude them from practicing before it, under 35 U.S.C. § 2(b)(2)(D) and 35 U.S.C. § 32; disciplinary hearings are conducted under 37 C.F.R. part 11 (subpart C) and 5 U.S.C. § 556 by an appointed hearing officer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations and prior decisions (e.g., Kroll v. Finnerty) explain the statutory basis; practitioners must receive notice and an opportunity for a hearing. Use the USPTO Rules and procedural rules to conduct and resolve disciplinary matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in OED disciplinary cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director bears the burden of proving alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing evidence is defined as proof between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt — evidence that produces a firm belief or conviction. Case citations (e.g., In re Johnson; Addington v. Texas) illustrate the standard. Apply this higher-than-preponderance standard when assessing whether alleged misconduct is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failing to answer a Complaint
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to timely file an answer constitutes an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notice of Docketing typically warns the respondent. Default may lead to findings deemed admitted and entry of sanctions (e.g., exclusion). Respondent behavior after service (communications, extensions) is still relevant but failure to answer exposes practitioner to default judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature requirements for trademark applications (personal entry)
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures must be personally entered by the named signatory; typing another’s electronic signature is not a valid signature under USPTO rules (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a),(c), 11.18(a); TMEP §611.01(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The person identified as the signatory must manually enter the electronic signature. Paralegals/assistants may not sign in place of the practitioner. Prior Board decisions (In re Dermahose; In re Cowan) reinforce that typing another's signature is no different than signing another's name on paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of electronic signature procedures in TEAS
rubrics_metrics.description: Three TEAS signature methods: DIRECT (signatory enters signature online at filing), ESIGN‑ON (preparer has third party sign the electronic signature for later filing), and H SIGN (electronic image of pen-and-ink signature submitted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DIRECT is default and typically ties the submission to an IP address/geolocation. ESIGN‑ON and H SIGN permit signing when the named signatory is remote. TICRS records the signature procedure and can show which method was used; signature method affects evidence about who actually signed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 11.18 certification obligations (reasonable inquiry)
rubrics_metrics.description: A signatory certifies under 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(b)(2) that, after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances, (i) the paper is not presented for an improper purpose; (ii) legal contentions are warranted or nonfrivolous; (iii) factual contentions have evidentiary support or are likely to after investigation; and (iv) denials are warranted on the evidence or reasonably based on lack of information or belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must make a reasonable inquiry before signing. Failure to undertake such an inquiry (e.g., regarding specimen authenticity or use-in-commerce) violates §11.18 and supports disciplinary findings. The standard ties signature to substantive verification duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimen and §1(a) trademark application requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To allege use under §1(a), an application must include an acceptable specimen showing the mark as actually used in commerce for each class identified (15 U.S.C. § 1051(a); 37 C.F.R. §§ 2.34(a)(1)(iv), 2.56(a); TMEP §§904, 904.07(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners can refuse registrations when specimens do not show current use (examples: mockups, altered images, unavailable products on website, screenshots that do not permit purchase). Practitioners must verify specimens are demonstrative of actual use before filing §1(a) applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule and its implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective Aug 3, 2019, foreign-domiciled trademark applicants must be represented by a U.S.-licensed attorney in good standing (37 C.F.R. § 2.11); the rule aims to improve accuracy and integrity of filings (e.g., specimens, signatures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners handling foreign-domiciled applicants must ensure compliance with U.S. Counsel Rule—including scrutinizing specimens and signatures—because failures can implicate unauthorized practice and integrity of the register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of TICRS and TESS data as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: TICRS records date/time when a document is created/submitted, the signature procedure used, and the IP address of the computer used; TESS is publicly available to search filings and identify where a practitioner is named.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IP addresses and timing patterns in TICRS can be used to infer whether a named signatory personally signed documents (e.g., multiple filings from different geolocations within minutes is evidence that the signatory did not personally sign them). TESS can identify the universe of filings listing a practitioner as attorney of record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to update address of record and related obligations (37 C.F.R. § 11.11)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must maintain a current §11.11 mailing address with the Office; failure to update the address (or respond to notices sent to address of record) can be an additional rule violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OED mailings and RFIs are sent to the §11.11 address; practitioners who fail to update the address may forfeit timely responses and cooperation claims. Timely receipt (certified mail returns) and failure to respond are evidentiary for noncooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to cooperate with OED investigations (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not fail to cooperate with the Office of Enrollment and Discipline in an investigation of a matter before it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-response to RFIs, ignoring interviews, failing to produce documents, or representing intent to cooperate but not doing so are violations. Prior case law (In re Ho; In re Glazer) supports exclusion for willful noncooperation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on false statements and obligation to correct (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly make a false statement of fact or law to a court or fail to correct a false statement of material fact or law previously made to a court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing another to sign the practitioner's name on USPTO documents where the Office will rely on them constitutes making/allowing false statements; the practitioner must correct known falsities (e.g., notify Trademark Operations of false signatures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on offering known false evidence and remedial duties (37 C.F.R. § 11.303(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not knowingly offer evidence known to be false; if material evidence is known to be false the practitioner must take reasonable remedial measures, including disclosure to the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a practitioner learns that filings or declarations bearing their signature are false, they must take remedial steps (e.g., disclosure to Trademark Operations). Failure to do so violates §11.303(a)(3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing false signatures on filings or otherwise misrepresenting who signed documents constitutes dishonesty/fraud. Such conduct is an aggravating factor and supports exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: It is professional misconduct for a practitioner to engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing false signatures, failing to inquire about specimen authenticity, failing to notify OED of false signatures, and failing to respond to the Office impede the administration of justice and warrant severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule requiring diligence and promptness in representing clients (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duties include ensuring filings are properly signed, having adequate review procedures, determining proper filing basis (§1(a) vs §1(b)), and verifying specimens. Lack of adequate review or supervisory procedures violates §11.103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions factors to consider (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining sanctions, the Court must consider: (1) whether the practitioner violated duties owed to client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether conduct was intentional/knowing/negligent; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury caused; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these four factors holistically: assess duties breached, mental state, actual/potential harm (harm need not be actual), and aggravators/mitigators (ABA STANDARDS guidance). The primary purpose of discipline is protection of public and administration of justice, not punishment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (ABA STANDARDS §§ 9.22, 9.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include dishonest/selfish motive, pattern of misconduct, multiple violations, bad faith obstruction, submission of false evidence, and substantial experience; a mitigating factor may be absence of prior disciplinary record (STANDARDS §9.32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate and weigh aggravators (e.g., dishonesty, pattern, obstruction) and any mitigators. Presence of multiple aggravators typically increases severity (e.g., exclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of mental state (intentional, knowing, negligent) and its impact on discipline (STANDARDS §3.0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mental state affects culpability: intent = acting with conscious objective to accomplish a result; knowing = conscious awareness of nature/circumstances without intent to achieve result; negligent = failure to be aware. Intentional/knowing conduct is sanctioned more severely than negligent conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine practitioner’s mens rea from conduct and admissions; knowing or intentional failures to act (e.g., allowing false signatures and failing to disclose) justify harsher discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm/potential injury consideration (actual or potential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harm from violations need not be actual; potential injury (e.g., jeopardized applications/registrations, risk to integrity of the trademark register) suffices when evaluating sanction severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: false signatures on many applications can expose clients to cancellation of registrations and integrity risks for the public; quantify scope (e.g., 1,400 filings) to assess gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and effect of exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusion from practice before the USPTO is an available sanction; excluded practitioners are eligible to apply for reinstatement no earlier than five years from the effective date, subject to 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 and compliance conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclusion bars practice in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters before the USPTO. Reinstatement eligibility and conditions are governed by regulation; consider remedial measures and rehabilitation evidence if reinstatement is sought.
